paras: The lynching of Wallace Mitchell took place at Syracuse, Hamilton County, Kansas, early on June 27, 1888, when a crowd of a hundred or more men took him from jail and hanged him for the murder of a twelve-year-old boy, Oscar Johnson. The men got in after the sheriff fled with the keys and hanged Mitchell from a telegraph pole where the killing had occurred. Many papers reported it as one of four Kansas lynchings in twenty-four hours.

Mitchell was accused of attacking August Johnson and his son with an ax as they slept by their wagon at Syracuse on the night of June 9, killing the boy, wounding the father, and robbing him. Held at Trinidad, Colorado, on a horse-stealing charge, he was brought back by Sheriff Huffman on June 26. In an interview that day he said that Oscar Johnson, August's brother, had proposed the killing; the Wichita Eagle's correspondent wrote that no one believed this and warned that "the people may forestall the courts."

That afternoon, before Justice Waggoner, Mitchell pleaded guilty to the murder and the attempted murder and was remanded to jail for the September term. A Garden City telegram said he told the story in front of the dead boy's mother, and that when the sheriff called on citizens to help defend the jail, no one came.

About midnight a body of men, put at "a hundred or more" in the Syracuse dispatch and at 150 in the Garden City telegram, gathered at the railroad water tank and went under a captain to the jail. The sheriff refused to give up his prisoner, and when some of the men brought railroad iron to batter the doors, he left. Pursuers caught him, but he had thrown the keys away; once they were found, Mitchell was brought out.

At the scene of the killing Mitchell said that Oscar Johnson had no part in the crime, and according to the Syracuse dispatch he said the sheriff of Las Animas County, Colorado, had helped him make up the earlier story. He prayed aloud for nearly an hour while many in the crowd knelt, and at about 1:30 a.m. he was hanged from the crosspiece of a telegraph pole.

The coroner held an inquest that morning, but according to the Garden City telegram "no one could be found who knew anything about it." Mitchell's friends said they did not want his remains, and he was to be buried at Syracuse. The coverage does not report any arrests. The Syracuse dispatch ended, "The verdict of the people sustains the lynching," and the Barbour County Index, in his former home county, called Mitchell and his brother "hard cases."

The full Syracuse dispatch ran in the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer on June 28 and in the Red Cloud Chief as late as July 6. A short wire ran from Emporia to Fort Worth and Atlanta, and the Garden City telegram appeared in the Richmond Dispatch.

Most headlines treated the hanging as deserved punishment: the Globe placed the mob's gathering under "Summary Justice," and the Wheeling paper said Mitchell's "Cold Blooded Recital of the Deed Arouses Uncontrollable Indignation Among the People." The Washington Critic, reprinted in the Delaware Ledger, described the crowd as acting with "all the deliberateness and solemnity of a regular court."

A Kansas City dispatch listed the case under "Four Lynchings in Kansas" and said that across the state "lynch law was the only remedy on hand." Briefer items on the same run called the two men lynched at Chetopa "negroes" but gave no race for Mitchell. The only condemnation found was an Iowa Citizen paragraph, reprinted in the Abbeville Press and Banner, that called the Kansas lynchings "a damnable outrage."

The Wheeling paper had Mitchell plead guilty to murdering August Johnson, and a Chicago paper named the victim "Albert Johnson." Only the Kansas City dispatch said the crowd dragged him "half dead" to the scene and riddled his body with bullets; the two dispatches from the scene describe a hanging alone. Some briefs placed the lynching on Tuesday night, June 26, rather than early on June 27.

accounts.label: Syracuse dispatch
accounts.gist: After his guilty plea, a hundred or more men under a captain demanded the prisoner, chased the sheriff, found the discarded keys, let Mitchell pray and confess at the murder site, and hanged him from a telegraph pole at 1:30 a.m.; 'the verdict of the people sustains the lynching.'

accounts.label: Garden City telegram
accounts.gist: The sheriff stood guard alone after no citizen answered his call; 150 men took Mitchell, knelt with him through nearly an hour of prayer, and hanged him; the inquest found no one who knew anything.

accounts.label: Kansas City summary
accounts.gist: Enraged citizens took Mitchell from the officers, dragged him half dead to the scene, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets, the first of four Kansas lynchings in a day.

accounts.label: Home-county paper
accounts.gist: The Barbour County Index described the crime and lynching briefly and said the end of Mitchell and his brother was no surprise to those who knew them.

framing.detail: The Syracuse dispatch called the prisoner's account a 'fiendish deed', headed the mob's action 'Summary Justice', and closed 'The verdict of the people sustains the lynching.'
Short wire items under heads such as 'Hanged Even in Kansas', 'The Scene of Crime' and 'Hanged by a Mob' ran in Kansas, Texas, Montana, Georgia and Wyoming papers.
Kansas City dispatches treated Mitchell's death as one of four Kansas lynchings caused by a law under which no condemned murderer was legally hanged.
The Washington Critic, reprinted by the Delaware Ledger, described the crowd's 'deliberateness and solemnity' without condemning it.
An Iowa Citizen paragraph reprinted in the Abbeville Press and Banner called the Kansas lynchings, including the Syracuse one, 'a damnable outrage'.
